rule_summary: Applicants must be at least 18 years old.
No fixed upper age is set. The page says the maximum age is decided by the best interests of the child.
People of any relationship status may apply, including common-law and same-sex couples. Applicants who live together must have been in a stable relationship for at least 12 months.
Applicants must be residents of Alberta.
Applicants must be financially stable.
notes: No income figure is given.

rule_summary: Applicants must be physically and mentally able to care for children safely. They must have had no major illness or trauma in the past 12 months.
notes: A medical reference is part of the application.

rule_summary: Applicants must not have taken on another child in the past year. They must not be expecting a child through pregnancy or adoption.
notes: The page also asks for a residence separate from other caregivers.

rule_summary: A criminal record check and an intervention record check are needed for everyone over 18 in the household. Both must be up to date at each yearly renewal.
notes: Foster Care Handbook dated 29 October 2021; it says it is not policy. The current Become a foster caregiver page also lists both checks.

rule_summary: Applicants complete a home study during screening. Screening also covers a medical reference, personal references and an environmental safety assessment.
notes: The page does not name the home study model.

rule_summary: Orientation training of 24 hours is mandatory before fostering. In a two-parent home both parents attend all sessions.
notes: From the 2021 handbook. The current Become a foster caregiver page calls it Caregiver Pre-Service Training and gives no hours. Alberta pays $450 after pre-service training (support page).

rule_summary: Level 1 core training is 31 courses of 3 hours each, done over 4 years. Emergency first aid and infant CPR are renewed every 3 years.
notes: 93 hours is our total of 31 courses of 3 hours, spread over 4 years. From the 2021 handbook; may have changed.

rule_summary: Ongoing training is a regulated requirement for foster caregivers. Each caregiver family builds a learning plan with their support worker.
notes: Training is offered every year in person and online.

rule_summary: The licence states the most children who may live in the home. A new Level 1 home may have up to 2 foster children, and a Level 2 home up to 4.
notes: 4 is the Level 2 maximum; Level 1 is 2. The caregivers' own children and respite of up to 2 weeks do not count. From the 2021 handbook.

rule_summary: Each child needs their own bed and enough space, in a room with a window. Rooms must not have locks on the outside.
notes: From the environmental safety assessment section of the 2021 handbook.

rule_summary: New foster homes are reassessed 6 months after they are licensed. After that they are reassessed every year.
Foster homes are licensed as residential facilities, and licensing is done every year. Renewal needs an annual evaluation, a renewal application, and current checks, insurance and safety assessment.
legal_citation: Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act, s. 105.2 (as cited in the handbook)
notes: From the 2021 handbook. The Act section was cited by the handbook, not read.

rule_summary: Basic maintenance for foster care, kinship care and supports for permanency is paid per day by age. The lowest rate is $26.00 a day for ages 0 to 1.
notes: Rates rise with age to $39.66 a day for ages 16 to 17. A $2.82 daily babysitting and relief amount is added. Schedule dated 18 February 2026. Supports for permanency covers some adoptions.

rule_summary: Foster caregivers must be at least 19 years old.
notes: Page last updated 20 October 2026.

rule_summary: Foster caregivers must be residents of British Columbia.
Single people, couples and families of all kinds may apply, with or without their own children.
notes: Booklet is undated.

rule_summary: Applicants do not need to own a home.
notes: Booklet is undated.

rule_summary: Applicants do not need to be stay-at-home parents.
notes: Booklet is undated.

rule_summary: Criminal record checks cover the applicant and everyone 18 or over in the home or with unsupervised access. Child welfare records and any time over 6 months outside British Columbia are also checked.
notes: The page says a criminal or child welfare record does not automatically prevent approval.

rule_summary: A resource worker completes a home study through several in-home interviews. Topics include personal history, parenting, relationships, lifestyle and the home.
notes: The undated booklet says the home study averages 4 to 6 interviews with every adult in the home: https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/family-and-social-supports/foster-parenting/foster_parenting_booklet_web.pdf

rule_summary: Applicants must finish online pre-service training before approval. It takes about 35 hours, self-paced over 12 weeks.
notes: The undated booklet names it PRIDE pre-service training, in 10 modules, for all adults in the home who will give care.

rule_summary: Ongoing training is required and expected of all foster caregivers.
notes: No hours are given. Booklet is undated.

rule_summary: A monthly maintenance payment is made for each child by age. The lowest rate is $1,549.20 a month for ages 0 to 11.
notes: Ages 12 to 19: $1,726.33 a month. Service payments for Levels 1 to 3 are paid on top. Page last updated 8 January 2026.

rule_summary: Two adults in a home can both be foster parents only if they are married or living common-law.
legal_citation: Child and Family Services Standards Manual, s. 1.5.2
notes: Standard approved 30 June 2022. The manual links this to Canada Revenue Agency rulings.

rule_summary: An application must include a criminal record check and a child abuse registry check for the applicant and every adult living with them. Each check must be dated within 3 months.
legal_citation: Foster Homes Licensing Regulation, M.R. 18/99, s. 3(2)(a)
notes: s. 3(2)(b) also requires consent to a prior contact check. Consolidation current from 12 December 2025.

rule_summary: The licensing agency must consider the checks and references and be satisfied adults in the home pose no risk. The proposed home must be inspected.
legal_citation: Foster Homes Licensing Regulation, M.R. 18/99, s. 3(4)
notes: The standards manual (s. 1.5.2) refers to a home study but does not name a model.

rule_summary: The licensing agency must give each applicant an orientation. This does not apply when the foster child is already personally known to the applicant.
legal_citation: Foster Homes Licensing Regulation, M.R. 18/99, s. 3(3)
notes: No hours are set. The standards manual says the Kinship and Foster Family Network of Manitoba offers an orientation.

rule_summary: Agencies and their mandating authorities are expected to provide ongoing training for foster parents.
legal_citation: Child and Family Services Standards Manual, s. 1.5.1
notes: No hours are set.

rule_summary: A foster home may be licensed for no more than 4 children, unless all the foster children are siblings. It may care for no more than 7 children and dependent adults in total, unless approved.
legal_citation: Foster Homes Licensing Regulation, M.R. 18/99, s. 7(1), (3) and (4)
notes: s. 7(5): no more than 2 infants and no more than 3 children under 5, unless approved. Children placed by other agencies count (s. 7(2)).

rule_summary: A foster child over 2 must not share a bedroom with an adult. A foster child over 5 must not share with a person of the opposite sex.
legal_citation: Foster Homes Licensing Regulation, M.R. 18/99, s. 25
notes: A basement may be used for sleeping only with fire and health authority approval.

rule_summary: A foster home licence is valid for 1 year.
legal_citation: Foster Homes Licensing Regulation, M.R. 18/99, s. 3(5)
notes: The licence ends earlier if it moves to another agency under s. 13.1.

rule_summary: A home should not be licensed unless a foster parent lives there at least five 24-hour days a week.
legal_citation: Child and Family Services Standards Manual, s. 1.5.2

rule_summary: Basic maintenance is paid per day by age band and location. The lowest rate is $24.32 a day for ages 0 to 10 south of the 53rd parallel.
notes: Scanned attachment titled Foster Care Rate 25/26, hosted by the Kinship and Foster Family Network of Manitoba. Highest is $35.75 a day (ages 11 to 17, north of 53 with no road access). A February 2025 news report gave a range of $24.32 to $34.72: https://www.mysteinbach.ca/news/15133/province-improves-support-for-children-in-care-with-increase-to-maintenance-rates/

rule_summary: A person aged 19 or older may apply to the Minister to approve a foster home.
legal_citation: Child and Youth Social Services Regulation, N.B. Reg. 2024-6, s. 12(1)
notes: Regulation filed 26 January 2024 under the Child and Youth Well-Being Act.

rule_summary: The Minister approves a foster home if the applicant meets the criteria and standards. A home study evaluation decides whether the services meet them.
notes: The regulation does not name a model. A 2013 provincial release (seen in search results only) said New Brunswick adopted SAFE.

rule_summary: Applicants who are not kin must have completed child and youth placement development training. They may instead complete it as soon as circumstances permit.
notes: The regulation gives no curriculum or hours.

rule_summary: Applicants who are not kin must give at least 3 references from people not related to them.
Homes for children who are not kin need a bedroom fully enclosed by floor-to-ceiling walls. If children share, each child needs their own bed.
notes: A child may not share if their care plan says so (s. 14(3)).

rule_summary: Homes must meet public health and fire prevention standards, have a first aid kit and keep medicines and chemicals out of reach. Rules also cover firearms, pools and animals.
notes: The Minister checks the standards with at least one home visit (s. 14(4)).

rule_summary: Homes for children who are not kin must be insured against loss of or damage to property.
A Social Development check, criminal record check and vulnerable sector check are done before a person becomes a foster or adoptive parent. Foster parents are checked again every 5 years.
legal_citation: General Regulation, N.B. Reg. 2024-4, s. 3(2)
notes: Checks are also repeated when the Minister gets information that may affect suitability. Checks need the person's consent (s. 3(1)).

rule_summary: At least one applicant must be 25 or older. A person close to 25 may start training, but no child is placed before their 25th birthday.
legal_citation: Protection and In Care Policy and Procedures Manual, policy 4.5
notes: Policy last revised 9 June 2025. The Foster a Future site says applicants must be at least 25: https://www.fosterafuture.ca/who-can-foster/

rule_summary: Single people or couples, with or without children, may apply. For a couple together less than 1 year, the social worker assesses how stable the relationship is.
legal_citation: Protection and In Care Policy and Procedures Manual, policy 4.5

rule_summary: Applicants must be residents of Newfoundland and Labrador.
Foster parents may own their home or rent.
Foster parents may stay at home, work outside the home or be retired.
Applicants complete a budget form and review their finances with a social worker. They are not approved if they would rely on foster payments for their own day-to-day costs.
legal_citation: Protection and In Care Policy and Procedures Manual, policy 4.5

rule_summary: Everyone in the home aged 12 or over needs a criminal record check; those 18 or over also need a vulnerable sector check. A child protection clearance check covers everyone in the home.
legal_citation: Protection and In Care Policy and Procedures Manual, policy 4.5
notes: Applicants are not approved if anyone has a conviction for a child-related crime. Checks repeat every 5 years (policy 4.12).

rule_summary: A social worker assesses applicants with the Guide for PRIDE Foster Home Assessments. Everyone living in the home takes part.
legal_citation: Protection and In Care Policy and Procedures Manual, policy 4.5
notes: PRIDE is a licensed programme; this row names it only.

rule_summary: Applicants complete 9 PRIDE pre-service sessions of 3 hours each. They can be done in person or online at their own pace.
notes: 27 hours is our total of 9 sessions of 3 hours.

rule_summary: Specialised foster homes must also complete PRIDE in-service, NVCI and ASIST training. Training needs are discussed at each annual review.
legal_citation: Protection and In Care Policy and Procedures Manual, policy 4.5.1
notes: Regular foster homes are required to complete PRIDE pre-service; other courses are encouraged. NVCI is Nonviolent Crisis Intervention; ASIST is Applied Suicide Intervention Skills Training.

rule_summary: A regular foster home may be approved for at most 3 children or youth, and a specialised home for at most 2. A manager may approve more for sibling groups.
legal_citation: Protection and In Care Policy and Procedures Manual, policy 4.10
notes: Policy last revised 28 June 2019.

rule_summary: Approval is reviewed every year from the date of first approval. The foster home agreement is signed again every 5 years.
legal_citation: Protection and In Care Policy and Procedures Manual, policy 4.12
notes: Policy last revised 28 June 2019.

rule_summary: Applicants give letters from 3 people not related to them who have known them for at least 3 years. A community contact also gives a verbal reference.
legal_citation: Protection and In Care Policy and Procedures Manual, policy 4.5

rule_summary: From 1 June 2026 the basic foster care rate is $1,010 a month per child on the island. It is higher in Labrador and remote Labrador.
notes: Labrador $1,160; remote Labrador $1,310. Block funding, level fees and an $85 Children's Special Allowance are paid on top. The page shows no age bands.

rule_summary: Foster caregiver and adoption applicants must be 19 or older.
legal_citation: Child and Family Wellbeing Policy Manual 2025, policies 4.9 and 4.10

rule_summary: Applicants must be Canadian citizens or permanent residents and live in Nova Scotia.
legal_citation: Child and Family Wellbeing Policy Manual 2025, policies 4.9 and 4.10

rule_summary: Applicants may be single, married or common-law. Two people who are married or common-law and live together must apply as a couple.
legal_citation: Child and Family Wellbeing Policy Manual 2025, policies 4.9 and 4.10

rule_summary: Applicants must complete appropriate background checks. They must be willing to discuss the results and how they relate to their circumstances.
legal_citation: Child and Family Wellbeing Policy Manual 2025, policies 4.9 and 4.10
notes: The policy does not list which checks. Its glossary defines criminal record and vulnerable sector checks.

rule_summary: An assessor approved by Child and Family Wellbeing interviews applicants, household members and references. An assessment is valid for 2 years.
legal_citation: Child and Family Wellbeing Policy Manual 2025, policy 4.11
notes: The approval decision states the number and ages of children assessed as a match.

rule_summary: Assessments are usually completed within 4 to 6 months of starting.
legal_citation: Child and Family Wellbeing Policy Manual 2025, policy 4.11
notes: Standardised training comes before the assessment (policy 4.12).

rule_summary: All applicants attend the PRIDE pre-service programme, which runs for 9 weeks.
notes: The permits directory entry names the former Department of Community Services and may be dated. Policy 4.12 of the 2025 manual requires standardised training for all applicants but names no curriculum.

rule_summary: Foster caregivers complete initial and ongoing training to build 5 set competencies.
legal_citation: Child and Family Wellbeing Policy Manual 2025, policy 7.17
notes: No hours are set.

rule_summary: Foster caregivers are reviewed every year to confirm ongoing approval. Reviews also happen 6 months after the first placement.
legal_citation: Child and Family Wellbeing Policy Manual 2025, policy 7.19
notes: The provincial permits directory lists the approval as having no expiry or renewal: https://novascotia.ca/sns/paal/comserv/paal058.asp

rule_summary: An agency must not approve a foster home unless it meets the foster home policy approved by the Minister.
legal_citation: Children and Family Services Regulations, s. 32(2)
notes: Unofficial consolidation.

rule_summary: Foster caregivers receive block funding every 2 weeks, set by the child's level of need and the number of children. The policy gives no amounts.
legal_citation: Child and Family Wellbeing Policy Manual 2025, policy 7.14
notes: A November 2021 release announced a $15 a day per diem increase: https://news.novascotia.ca/en/2021/11/03/foster-care-redesign-increases-support-children-foster-families Current amounts not found.

rule_summary: All foster parents and adults in the home need a criminal record check before final approval. It is updated every 2 years while the home is open.
legal_citation: Child and Family Services Standards and Procedures Manual, Standard 7.4
notes: Consent forms cover adults 19 and older. Listed relevant charges lead to rejection; fingerprints may be needed.

rule_summary: Workers check child protection records for applicants, including other provinces or territories where they lived.
legal_citation: Child and Family Services Standards and Procedures Manual, Standard 7.3

rule_summary: A worker completes the Foster Home Study form by interviewing the applicants and everyone else living in the home.
legal_citation: Child and Family Services Standards and Procedures Manual, Standard 7.3; Child and Family Services Act, s. 62(3)

rule_summary: The evaluation must be done within 45 days of a complete application package. Applicants are told the outcome within 14 days of the home study interviews.
legal_citation: Child and Family Services Standards and Procedures Manual, Standard 7.3
notes: Delays because of missing documents must be recorded in case notes.

rule_summary: The application package includes 3 non-family references, a medical report and an RCMP criminal record.
legal_citation: Child and Family Services Standards and Procedures Manual, Standard 7.3

rule_summary: No foster parent may receive or keep more than 3 infants under 1 year old for over 24 hours.
legal_citation: Child and Family Services Standards and Procedures Manual, Standard 7.12; Child and Family Services Act, s. 67
notes: This limit is for infants only. No overall limit was found in the standards read.

rule_summary: Workers must give foster parents chances to take skill-based training. This includes PRIDE modules and courses on specific topics.
legal_citation: Child and Family Services Standards and Procedures Manual, Standard 7.14
notes: No hours or pre-approval training requirement are stated.

rule_summary: Workers review every foster home each year. The review includes interviews with everyone in the home and a check of the home.
legal_citation: Child and Family Services Standards and Procedures Manual, Standard 7.6

rule_summary: The daily foster care rate varies by community, from $33 a day in Yellowknife. An age-of-child amount of $5 to $7 a day is added.
notes: Highest community rate is $65 (Sachs Harbour). Subsidized adoption gets 90% of the foster care rate.

rule_summary: Screening for new foster homes includes criminal record checks and vulnerable sector checks of adults living in the home.
notes: From the May 2023 Auditor General of Canada report, which lists required screening steps. The Department's own rule text was not read.

rule_summary: A 2024 recruitment notice asks for criminal record and vulnerable sector checks for all adults over 19 in the household.
notes: The site returned HTTP 403 to our polite reader, so this row comes from search result summaries.

rule_summary: Screening for new foster homes includes a home study, which assesses whether the home is suitable and includes a visit.
notes: From the May 2023 Auditor General of Canada report. A foster home agreement is also required.

rule_summary: Applicants submit an application form, a medical form from a physician or nurse, an RCMP criminal record check and 3 reference letters.
notes: The site returned HTTP 403 to our polite reader, so this row comes from search result summaries.

rule_summary: Family Services lists a foster parent orientation and pre-service training course. No hours were found.
notes: The site returned HTTP 403 to our polite reader, so this row comes from search result summaries.

rule_summary: From 1 April 2020, basic per diem rates were $58 to $62 a day, set by community zone.
notes: The site returned HTTP 403 to our polite reader, so this row comes from search result summaries. A November 2026 release says foster families got a 45% pay increase backdated to 1 April 2026; new rates not found: https://www.gov.nu.ca/en/newsroom/government-nunavut-accepts-auditor-generals-findings-reaffirms-commitment-strengthening

rule_summary: The Children's Aid Society of Ottawa asks that applicants be over 18.
notes: No minimum age was found in O. Reg. 156/18. Each children's aid society sets its own criteria, so others may differ.

rule_summary: The province says foster parents can come from all groups in Ontario, including any marital status.
notes: Page updated 2 March 2026.

rule_summary: The province says foster parents can come from all groups, including any level of financial income.
notes: The Children's Aid Society of Ottawa asks that applicants be financially stable: https://casott.on.ca/services/fostering/

rule_summary: A licensee must not place a child if the home would then have more than 4 foster children. No more than 2 foster children may be under age 2.
notes: Exceptions in s. 125(2) to (4) were not read in full.

rule_summary: A foster child's sleeping room needs a window and a privacy barrier. It cannot be in an unfinished attic or basement, a hall or a detached building.
notes: A Director may approve other arrangements (s. 121(9)). Each foster child needs a suitable bed and clean mattress (s. 125(1)).

rule_summary: People seeking to be foster parents, and adults 18 or over living with them, must provide a broad police record check. Foster parents renew it at least every 3 years.
notes: Table to s. 121, items 15 to 18. Child welfare record checks appear on society pages, for example https://cassdg.ca/en/foster/who-can-be-a-foster-caregiver/

rule_summary: Societies must use the SAFE home study, or HEART for caregivers of Indigenous children. A worker doing SAFE must have taken the OACAS SAFE course.
legal_citation: Policy Directive CW 003-20 (issued under CYFSA s. 42)
notes: Applies to foster, kinship, customary care and adoption applicants. O. Reg. 156/18, s. 121(2) sets interviews, references, a health statement and a home visit.

rule_summary: The assessment needs 3 references for a single applicant or 5 for a couple. Applicants cannot be references for themselves or each other.
Applicants must finish PRIDE or SPIRIT pre-service training before approval. They also need standard first aid with infant and child CPR.
legal_citation: Policy Directive RL 001-23; O. Reg. 156/18, s. 121(1)
notes: SPIRIT is used with HEART for caregivers of Indigenous children (CW 003-20).

rule_summary: The OACAS says PRIDE pre-service is 9 modules and 27 hours. It is used for kinship care, fostering and adoption.
notes: York Region CAS also describes PRIDE as 27 hours: https://www.yorkcas.org/foster-caregivers/

rule_summary: Within 6 months of approval, foster parents take 3 courses of at least 4 hours each. These cover First Nations, Inuit and Métis culture, trauma-informed care, and caring for Black children.
legal_citation: Policy Directive RL 001-23
notes: 12 hours is our total of 3 courses of at least 4 hours. First Nations, Inuit and Métis foster parents are exempt from the cultural course. Each learning plan is reviewed at least every 3 months (O. Reg. 156/18, s. 122(4)).

rule_summary: The licensee reviews each foster parent and home 12 months after approval and every 12 months after that.
notes: Foster care licences are issued to agencies, not to foster parents.

rule_summary: The Children's Aid Society of Ottawa says the assessment usually takes 4 to 6 months.
notes: The OACAS says a SAFE home study can take 4 to 6 months and is generally valid for up to 2 years: https://www.oacas.org/childrens-aid-child-protection/fostering/

rule_summary: York Region CAS pays a daily, non-taxable reimbursement for each child. The amount is not given, and no provincial rate schedule was found.
notes: Rates appear to be set by each children's aid society.

rule_summary: Applicants must have reached the age of majority. The English version of the page says 18 or older.
notes: French page, updated 2 September 2025. Criteria were eased in May 2025.

rule_summary: Anyone may become a foster family, whatever their civil status. A foster family may be a single person, a couple or a family.
notes: The second sentence is from the description page: https://www.quebec.ca/famille-et-soutien-aux-personnes/enfance/famille-accueil/description-famille-accueil

rule_summary: Applicants must be Canadian citizens or permanent residents.
Applicants must not have declared personal bankruptcy in the past 3 years. They provide a certificate of financial solvency.
notes: The solvency certificate is listed on the procedure page: https://www.quebec.ca/famille-et-soutien-aux-personnes/enfance/famille-accueil/demarche

rule_summary: Applicants must have home insurance as an owner or a tenant.
The person may work outside the home.
Bedrooms should preferably be private, with a window, on the ground floor or upstairs. A basement bedroom is accepted if it meets safety standards.
A foster family can take in 1 to 9 young people placed by a public institution.
notes: Page updated 25 July 2023. The legal source of the limit was not read.

rule_summary: Applicants and other adults in the home must have no criminal record linked to fostering duties. New applicants give proof of no impediment from a police check when asked.
notes: The police check is called a vérification d'absence d'empêchement (VAE). Applicants must also not have had a recognition suspended or revoked in the past 3 years.

rule_summary: In Capitale-Nationale, a psychosocial assessment takes 3 to 6 meetings and a visit to check the home. An approval committee then decides.
notes: Regional process; other regions may differ.

rule_summary: Applicants must hold current CPR and standard first aid certification from a recognised body.
notes: The Capitale-Nationale page also asks applicants to watch an information session first: https://www.ciusss-capitalenationale.gouv.qc.ca/services/famille-enfants-parents/adoption-famille-accueil/devenir-famille-accueil/comment-faire

rule_summary: Under the FFARIQ collective agreement, families get a daily rate per child by service level. Level 1 is $50.58 a day from 1 April 2026.
legal_citation: Entente collective FFARIQ 2023-2028, cl. 3-3.06 and 3-7.02
notes: This is a payment for services, not a basic maintenance rate. A daily operating-expenses allowance is added: $33.05 per child from 1 January 2025, indexed each January. Read from a scanned copy. Other associations' agreements may apply to some families.

rule_summary: Married, single, same-sex or common-law applicants may apply, with or without children.
notes: saskatchewan.ca blocks our reader in robots.txt, so the Saskatchewan Foster Families Association pages were used.

rule_summary: Foster homes can be owned or rented. They must be clean, furnished, in good repair and free from health and fire hazards.
A child in care may have their own bedroom or share with a child of the same gender and compatible age.
Ministry policy allows no more than 4 foster children in a home. Exceptions include emergencies, large sibling groups and children who lived there before.
notes: The 2021 SFFA handbook adds limits for children under 24 and 30 months and says exceptions are reviewed every 2 weeks: https://saskfosterfamilies.ca/files/pdfs/SFFA-Handbook-3rd-Edition-2021-09-28.pdf

rule_summary: Before approval, the Ministry checks its own records and gets criminal record and vulnerable sector checks for applicants and other adults 18 or over. These checks are repeated every 3 years.
notes: From the 2026 Provincial Auditor follow-up report, which describes Ministry practice.

rule_summary: Prospective foster parents take part in a family assessment home study, which includes PRIDE pre-service training.
notes: A Ministry social worker interviews applicants and checks references: https://saskfosterfamilies.ca/becoming-a-foster-parent/how-to-become-a-foster-parent

rule_summary: Pre-service training takes about 30 hours, followed by first aid and CPR training.
notes: The 2021 SFFA handbook lists PRIDE pre-service sessions 1 to 9 (27 hours) and a 3-hour Saskatchewan Aboriginal cultural component.

rule_summary: First-year training includes PRIDE Core modules 1 and 2 (21 hours) and first aid with CPR (17 hours). FASD (3 hours) and trauma training (6 hours) are also required.
notes: 47 hours is our total of the listed first-year items. First aid is renewed every 3 years. Handbook dated September 2021.

rule_summary: Each foster home is reviewed at least once each calendar year using the PRIDE Family Development Plan.
legal_citation: Children's Services Manual, s. 4.4.8
notes: Section dated October 2001, revised May 2009; copy hosted by SFFA. The Ministry also visits at least every 6 months.
